Volume 07 · Chapter 11

Accounting standards, disclosure and comparability

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v07-c10

By the endIdentify where accounting-policy differences require adjustment and dated source verification.

Capability and prerequisites

You can decide whether two accounting numbers describe comparable objects, make a supported common-basis adjustment, and preserve the difference between a policy, a revised estimate and an error. Use inventory cost flows, asset depreciation, group boundaries and internal eliminations, tax and accrual bridges, and linked forecasts. No knowledge of every accounting standard is assumed.

Two distributors report the same sales but different profits. One might have a better business, a different inventory cost convention, a different reporting perimeter, or a mistake. A ratio does not choose among those explanations. Comparability requires an evidence trail from an identified report to a defined adjustment and then through the linked statements.

1. Identify the report before comparing the number

IFRS Accounting Standards are issued by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB). U.S. GAAP denotes the applicable U.S. generally accepted accounting principles; FASB's Accounting Standards Codification is the authoritative source recognized by FASB for nongovernmental entities. A FASB Accounting Standards Update (ASU) communicates amendments; it is not itself the Codification. The actual ASU 2015-11 front matter makes this distinction. Neither framework's name determines every policy, estimate or reporting judgment.

Jurisdiction, entity type and filing status matter. For example, the SEC's Financial Reporting Manual, section 6310, describes the ability of a qualifying foreign private issuer to file IFRS-as-issued-by-the-IASB statements without U.S. GAAP reconciliation. It calls for the appropriate compliance statement and audit opinion; a vague “international standards” label is insufficient. That scoped U.S. filing accommodation does not establish that a U.S. domestic issuer, private company, bank or foreign subsidiary has the same requirements. The manual is staff guidance; inspect the applicable rule and current filing facts before making a filing conclusion.

A comparison record that another analyst can reproduce
FieldWhat to record and why
Entity and perimeterLegal issuer, consolidated group or separate company; acquisitions, disposals, NCI and discontinued businesses. A larger boundary can raise sales without organic growth.
TimePeriod start/end, 52/53-week calendar, annual versus interim, authorization/filing date and information available at the decision date.
Units and currencyThousands versus millions; presentation currency; any constant-currency method and the rate convention. A currency conversion alone does not align policies.
Framework and versionExact compliance wording, local adoption or endorsement, relevant standard/amendment, effective period and any disclosed early adoption.
Number and evidenceStatement line, note, table/paragraph, original or revised comparative, policy and estimation assumptions. Keep the report's title, URL, date and version.
Analytical treatmentTarget definition, equation, both opening and closing adjustments, tax/perimeter assumptions, and whether the result is reported, analyst-adjusted or still unknown.

Do not silently overwrite an original observation with a later restatement. A financial-history analysis may need the corrected series; a test of what investors could know needs the originally available version. Preserve both with an explicit mapping. “Not disclosed” is not zero, and “not comparable” can be the defensible result when an adjustment cannot be measured.

A dated source trap. The IFRS Foundation's IFRS 18 overview states an effective date of annual periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027, with earlier application permitted. IFRS 18 replaces IAS 1 and moves some requirements to IAS 8; the public IAS 8 page now uses the title Basis of Preparation of Financial Statements. An issued standard's current web title does not prove that a 2025 reporter adopted it. At this library's 6 October 2026 edition boundary, check the actual report's adoption note and the jurisdiction's implementation. The new presentation and management-defined-performance-measure requirements are not assumed to apply to every historical statement discussed here.

2. Locate the difference: recognition, measurement, presentation or disclosure

Recognition asks whether and when an item enters the statements. Measurement assigns its monetary amount. Presentation chooses a statement line, grouping or subtotal. Disclosure supplies explanations and supporting detail. These questions interact, but they are not interchangeable. Describing an uncertainty in a note does not by itself justify recognizing an asset; relabeling an expense does not remove its economic cost.

Suppose both companies paid 300 for goods and sold the same quantities. A cost-flow measurement difference can change inventory and profit without changing those payments. Alternatively, one company may combine delivery costs with cost of sales while another displays them below gross profit. A gross-margin comparison then needs the same numerator definition even if operating profit already agrees. If one company includes an acquired subsidiary for only three months, changing an expense label cannot repair the perimeter difference.

Start with the most specific applicable requirement and the actual transaction facts. The IAS 8 public overview describes the policy-selection hierarchy when no specific standard applies. This is not permission to choose whichever framework produces a preferred profit. A common-basis analyst calculation is also not an accounting-policy election by the issuer. Its purpose, evidence and limitations should be stated separately.

A practical adjustment sheet has one row per cause. For each row, record the reported amount, the target amount, the difference, affected accounts and whether cash actually changes. Sum causes only if they do not overlap. A second analyst should be able to reverse the sheet to recover the published statements. Reconcile assets minus liabilities to equity and reconcile profit to cash. A balanced sheet can still contain an unsupported assumption; the source note is part of the calculation.

3. Policy comparison without inventing cash

For interchangeable inventories, the IAS 2 overview identifies FIFO or weighted-average cost formulas. LIFO is not one of those formulas. The actual FASB ASU 2015-11 amendment text distinguishes U.S. inventory measured under LIFO/retail from inventory under other methods. Thus “IFRS and U.S. GAAP inventories mean the same thing” is unsafe. The sources establish this limited contrast, not an exhaustive comparison of inventory rules, tax elections, impairment or industry exceptions.

Let IF,t and IL,t be FIFO and LIFO carrying values for the same physical inventory and transaction history. Define the comparison reserve Rt = IF,t − IL,t. It is a valuation difference, not a cash account. With identical purchases Bt, no write-downs and no other inventory movements, each cost formula satisfies COGSt = It−1 + Bt − It. Subtraction gives

COGSF,t − COGSL,t = Rt−1 − Rt = −ΔRt.
ProfitF,t = ProfitL,t + ΔRt, when all other items and taxes are unchanged.

The ending reserve adjusts a stock; its change adjusts a period flow. This distinction prevents adding the entire accumulated difference to each year's income. No-tax equity changes by Rt when the inventory adjustment is the only balance-sheet difference. The opening equity difference Rt−1 plus the period profit difference ΔRt must equal that ending difference.

Worked example 1 — The same warehouse on two cost bases

Orion is an invented wholesaler. Money is kCU, thousands of currency units; quantities are thousands of identical units and prices are CU per unit. Opening cash is 500 and inventory is 100 units at 2, costing 200. Unchanged external liabilities are 100; share capital is 600 and RE zero, so 700 = 100 + 600. All goods are recoverable at cost. There is no tax, interest, depreciation, FX, dividend or acquisition. Every purchase, sale and operating expense is cash. Purchases occur before sales, followed by the operating payment in each fictional year.

Orion's unchanged economic transactions
YearPurchasesSalesOther operating payments
X1100 × 3 = 300120 × 5 = 60080
X2100 × 4 = 40090 × 6 = 54090

Use simple annual periodic FIFO and unit LIFO cost layers. These are two counterfactual measurement schedules for the same business, not a claim that LIFO is an IFRS election. FIFO removes the oldest costs first; LIFO removes the latest costs first. The cost assignment does not assert which physical box was shipped.

In X1, FIFO COGS is 100 × 2 + 20 × 3 = 260; the remaining 80 units cost 240. LIFO COGS is 100 × 3 + 20 × 2 = 340; the remaining 80 units cost 160. Profits are respectively 600 − 260 − 80 = 260 and 600 − 340 − 80 = 180. The reserve rises from zero to 80.

In X2, FIFO removes the old 80 at 3 and ten new units at 4: COGS 280, closing inventory 90 × 4 = 360 and profit 170. LIFO removes 90 new units at 4: COGS 360, closing layers 80 × 2 + 10 × 4 = 200 and profit 90. R2 = 160, but ΔR2 = 80. Adjusting LIFO profit 90 by 160 would report 250 and count an earlier year's difference again. The correct common-FIFO profit is 170.

Complete position and cash checks, kCU
MeasureX1 FIFOX1 LIFOX2 FIFOX2 LIFO
Closing cash720720770770
Closing inventory240160360200
Assets9608801130970
Liabilities100100100100
Equity: capital + retained profit8607801030870
Profit26018017090
Inventory increase40−4012040
CFO = profit − inventory increase2202205050

External cash verifies CFO directly: X1 gives 600 − 300 − 80 = 220; X2 gives 540 − 400 − 90 = 50. Changing the valuation schedule adds ΔR to profit and to the inventory increase, so those indirect-CFO changes cancel. Funding also works: cash after each purchase is 200 then 320, before sales arrive. The measurement adjustment creates no extra ability to pay a supplier.

This is a policy-only, no-tax comparison. In a real conversion, tax bases, deferred taxes, tax payments, inventory impairments, acquisitions and different reserve definitions may matter. A disclosed LIFO reserve is not necessarily defined against your chosen FIFO target; inspect the note. Do not apply the formula to an unexplained difference between two unrelated firms' inventory totals. If R falls, the profit adjustment can be negative; price increases alone do not guarantee rising reserves when old layers are liquidated.

4. Policy, new estimate or old error?

The IAS 8 overview separates policy changes, revised estimates arising from new information, and errors caused by not using reliable information available for the earlier statements. Its broad treatment is retrospective for policy changes and material prior-period errors, subject to transition provisions and practicability limits; estimate revisions operate prospectively. These are classifications of evidence, not labels management can choose to smooth profit.

Classification before calculation
QuestionIllustrative answerTreatment to investigate
Has the accounting basis changed?An allowed cost-flow policy changes, with a supported reason and applicable conditions.Policy change: inspect the governing transition rule and required opening-equity/comparative bridge.
Has the evidence about an uncertain amount changed?A new engineering assessment changes remaining useful life after proper earlier estimates.Estimate revision: use the carrying amount and revised facts from the change date.
Was relevant reliable information available but misused?A documented life was entered incorrectly and the error is material.Prior-period error: identify affected earlier periods and reconstruct corrected comparatives.
Has only the display changed?The same expense moves between two presentation lines.Reclassification: preserve the totals and identify any recast comparatives; do not invent income.

The detailed AASB 108 compilation applicable to periods beginning in 2023–2026 supplies an accessible, jurisdiction-labeled text incorporating IAS 8. Paragraphs 14–22 constrain policy changes and explain retrospective opening-equity adjustments; paragraphs 34–38 distinguish new evidence and prospective estimates; paragraphs 42–49 address material errors and disclosure. Australian-specific and simplified-disclosure provisions are not assumed to apply elsewhere. A switch is not justified merely because its result looks more attractive, and an adverse surprise does not by itself prove the original estimate was erroneous.

Worked example 2 — One machine, two different histories

This is a separate fictional no-tax case. A machine costing 120 kCU was bought for cash and made available for use on 1 January X1. Residual value is zero; straight-line depreciation was 120/6 = 20 per year under an initially recorded six-year life. After X2, accumulated depreciation is 40 and carrying amount is 80. No impairment or other asset movement occurs. Cash operating profit before depreciation is 100 in each year; there are no other accruals.

History A: new evidence. The original estimate was reasonable using information then available. A new assessment at the start of X3 gives three remaining years. Depreciate the remaining 80 over X3–X5: 80/3 each year. X1 and X2 stay at 20. X3 profit becomes 100 − 80/3 = 220/3 ≈ 73.333, and the machine ends X3 at 160/3 ≈ 53.333. Compared with the unrevised X3 profit of 80, the change is −20/3. No extra 20 is charged to recreate a history that did not occur.

History B: a material input error. Instead, suppose reliable contemporaneous documentation established a four-year life from the outset, but a data-entry mistake used six. The error is material; reliable reconstruction is practicable. Correct X1 and X2 depreciation to 30 each. Accumulated depreciation becomes 60 and the start-X3 carrying amount becomes 60. The cumulative asset and retained-earnings correction is −20, with no cash adjustment.

If X2 is the earliest comparative year displayed alongside X3, its opening machine balance changes from 100 to 90 and opening RE decreases by ten for the X1 error. X2 depreciation increases from 20 to 30, reducing X2 profit by another ten. Together these adjustments explain the ending-X2 reduction of 20. In the corrected X3 schedule, remaining life is two years and depreciation is 30; profit is 70. Charging the prior 20 again to X3 in addition to current depreciation would give 50 and distort the period's performance.

Schedules preserve the timing of information, kCU
CaseX1/X2 depreciationStart-X3 assetX3 depreciationX3 profitX3 CFO
Original schedule20 / 20802080100
A: new estimate20 / 208080/3220/3100
B: corrected history30 / 30603070100

In every row, CFO = profit + depreciation = 100. The purchase cash was paid at the start of X1, not recreated when a schedule changes. Yet equal current cash does not make the histories equivalent: asset consumption, evidence quality, future reported profit and comparatives differ. Both corrected and revised schedules ultimately depreciate total cost 120, with the specified timing.

A complete correction file identifies the error, evidence available at the original authorization date, affected lines, opening balances, current-period consequences and tax effects. Separate the issuer's required restatement from an analyst's pro forma comparison. Our materiality and practicability conclusions are stipulated; in an actual report they require analysis. The dated AASB text also distinguishes genuine inability to reconstruct from mere inconvenience and explains why the prior correction is excluded from discovery-period profit. This chapter does not infer intent from a correction.

5. Segments: management's view still needs a bridge

The IFRS 8 overview describes disclosures about different activities, economic environments, products, geography and major customers within its scope. A segment need not be a separate legal subsidiary. Under the detailed AASB 8 text incorporating IFRS 8, an operating segment has business activity, separately available financial information and results reviewed for resource allocation and performance by the chief operating decision maker (CODM). CODM is a function, not a required job title. Identifying operating segments precedes applying reportability and aggregation rules; we stipulate reportable segments in our case rather than infer them from convenient labels.

Segment measures can omit group costs or use internal allocation conventions. Ask what the CODM receives, which costs the measure includes, how transfers are priced and how totals reconcile. The actual FASB ASU 2023-07 adds significant segment-expense and other-segment-item disclosures for public entities in scope. It states annual effectiveness for fiscal years beginning after 15 December 2023, and interim effectiveness for fiscal years beginning after 15 December 2024, with early adoption allowed. The amendment retains a management perspective and provides reconciliation requirements; it does not turn every segment subtotal into consolidated net income.

Worked example 3 — From segment packages to group results

Another invented group, Vector, provides these X1 data in kCU. Hardware and Services are stipulated reportable segments. Hardware's 40 of transfers to Services is included in Hardware revenue and Services expenses. All transferred goods are sold externally or consumed in external services this year: no unrealized internal profit remains. All figures use the same period, currency and group boundary.

Vector's segment packet
MeasureHardwareServices
External revenue300200
Intersegment revenue400
Total segment revenue340200
Separately shown cost category22080
Separately shown payroll4050
Other included segment expenses2634
Reported segment profit5436
Segment assets180120

The other-expense reconciliation is 340 − 220 − 40 − 54 = 26 for Hardware and 200 − 80 − 50 − 36 = 34 for Services. “Other” is not automatically zero or a nonrecurring charge. Its composition needs an explanation even after the arithmetic balances.

Consolidated external revenue is 340 + 200 − 40 = 500. Reported segment profits sum to 90. The packet excludes corporate operating costs 20, share-based compensation expense ten and interest eight. Consolidated operating profit under the case's stated subtotal is 90 − 20 − 10 = 60; profit before tax is 52. Supplied income-tax expense is 13, giving net income 39. This is an income reconciliation; it supplies no tax-payment or CFO figure.

Do not subtract the transfer 40 again from the sum of segment profits. Eliminating both its revenue and matching expense has zero net effect here. Independently, total segment expenses are 286 + 164 = 450; after eliminating internal expense 40 and adding the unallocated 30, group operating expense is 440. External revenue 500 minus 440 confirms operating profit 60.

Corporate assets outside the segments are 50. Segment assets contain an internal receivable 20 that has a matching internal payable elsewhere in the group. Consolidated assets are 180 + 120 + 50 − 20 = 330. These supplied assets and the income bridge are not a complete balance sheet or cash-flow statement. Inventing liabilities, equity or cash generation from them would exceed the evidence.

Now change only the internal transfer price from 40 to 50, increasing the buyer's included cost by the same ten. Hardware profit becomes 64 and Services profit 26. Total segment profit remains 90; consolidated revenue and profit remain 500 and 39 after matching eliminations. A segment manager's apparent improvement can therefore reflect an allocation change rather than a group gain. If some goods remained unsold, the no-unrealized-margin assumption would fail and inventory-profit elimination would also be needed.

A second company may allocate the corporate 30 into its segment results. Comparing its segment profits with Vector's unallocated figures would favor Vector mechanically. Record the cost boundary before ranking margins. Likewise, a change in segment composition can break a time series even when group totals are unchanged. Use the issuer's recast comparatives or a supported mapping, and retain the originally published series. The dated AASB 8 reconciliation and comparative provisions and the U.S. amendment's recasting provisions provide scoped routes for further reading; the detailed exceptions and disclosure tests are not presumed identical across frameworks.

6. Turn disclosure evidence into an analytical decision

Read the primary statements together with the basis-of-preparation, material policy, estimation, segment, acquisition and restatement notes. Search for changes as well as levels. A method name without the range of assumptions may not explain a reported amount. For a life estimate, ask for the old and new lives, residual values, affected asset pool, timing and current-period effect. For an inventory bridge, ask for both reserves, the reserve's actual definition and any movements outside ordinary COGS.

Build comparisons in three layers. First preserve the published numbers. Next make separately justified measurement or presentation adjustments. Finally consider economic differences that an accounting adjustment cannot eliminate: product mix, capital intensity, customer risk, geography and business maturity. A common inventory formula does not make two firms equally efficient. Adjusting away a recurring cost does not show that owners no longer bear it.

Currency and calendar adjustments also require explicit models. A constant-currency revenue series asks what translation would have been under a specified rate convention; it does not identify how customers would have behaved without exchange-rate changes. A 53-week year cannot always be converted to 52 weeks by proportional scaling because sales are seasonal. Acquisitions change exposure dates and may change transfer pricing and accounting estimates as well as the reporting boundary. Request a nonoverlapping bridge instead of subtracting every plausible adjustment independently.

For a forecast, feed the adjusted opening stocks and period flows into the linked model together. Do not start with FIFO-adjusted inventory and unadjusted LIFO equity. Preserve uncertainty when the disclosures do not identify a unique adjustment: show a conditional range or exclude the affected ratio. A documented inability to compare is more informative than a precisely calculated ratio whose denominator belongs to another entity or date.

7. Reproducible comparison laboratory

Download the original case data and assumptions, standard-library benchmark, preserved output and README. Keep the files together and run python3 v07-c11-analysis.py. Numeric inputs and outputs use exact rational strings: "80/3" is exact, while a displayed decimal is an approximation. The program makes no network requests.

Rebuild the FIFO/LIFO layers, the evidence-dependent depreciation schedules and segment reconciliations before inspecting the answers. The laboratory reports both published-style bases and the analytical bridge; it never substitutes zero for missing numerical evidence. Try equal unit costs, full inventory liquidation, a different remaining useful life, or a matched internal transfer-price change. Explain which invariants survive and why. The model's cash checks apply to Orion's supplied purchase-before-sale dates; the segment packet contains no cash-flow model.

Exercises

  1. Audit the source boundary. An analyst labels a foreign issuer's 2025 Form 20-F “IFRS” because a data provider says so. A linked local report says “home-country standards based on IFRS”; no IASB-compliance statement, adoption note or auditor's report has been inspected. The analyst also applies IFRS 18 because its public page is available today. State what is and is not established, list the evidence required before claiming that U.S. GAAP reconciliation may be omitted, and explain how to select the applicable presentation version.
  2. Use the change in a reserve. A no-tax, all-cash trading case reports LIFO opening inventory 120, closing inventory 140, COGS 260 and profit 70. The opening and closing reserves, expressly defined as FIFO minus LIFO, are 30 and 45. No other inventory movement, working-capital change or noncash item exists. Derive FIFO purchases/COGS/inventory/profit, opening and closing equity adjustments, and CFO under each basis. Explain why adding 45 to current profit fails.
  3. Liquidate Orion's layers. Append X3 to Worked example 1: purchase nothing; sell all remaining 90 units for 5 CU each; pay other operating expense 50. Keep every other assumption. Compute profit under each basis, the reserve change, CFO, cash, assets and equity. Does a higher LIFO profit prove better X3 sales performance?
  4. Revise an estimate. A separate machine costs 150, has residual value 30 and an initially reasonable six-year straight-line life. After two full years, genuinely new evidence establishes two remaining years; the residual remains 30. There is no impairment or tax. Give the carrying amount at revision, new annual depreciation, current profit and CFO if cash operating profit before depreciation is 90 with no other accruals. State what happens to prior depreciation and identify the evidence distinguishing this from an error.
  5. Correct the period rather than smoothing it. Use History B in Worked example 2. Assume opening-X1 retained earnings are zero. No other transactions affect RE, and cash operating profit before depreciation was 100 in X1 and X2. X2 is the earliest comparative shown alongside X3. Give reported and corrected opening-X2 RE, X2 profit, closing-X2 RE and machine balances. Give the start-X3 correction and X3 profit. Explain the error in charging the entire prior correction to X3 profit.
  6. Reconcile the segment packet. Reconstruct Vector's other segment expenses, consolidated external revenue, operating profit, profit before tax, net income and assets. An analyst subtracts internal sales 40 from the 90 segment-profit sum, then subtracts corporate costs, share compensation and interest, obtaining PBT 12. Locate the double subtraction. Can net income 39 be called CFO?
  7. Repair a segment growth series. X1 originally reported segment A revenue 260 and B revenue 140. At the start of X2, an activity is moved from A to B. Its X1 revenue was 20; reliable comparable data are supplied. Current X2 revenues under the new structure are A 252 and B 168. There are no internal sales, acquisitions, currency or calendar differences. Recast X1 and calculate both segment growth rates and group growth. Compare with growth calculated from the unrecast figures; state whether the group requires a revenue correction.
  8. Separate a bridge from an economic claim. A group reports revenue 660 for a 53-week current year and 500 for a 52-week prior year. A reliable, nonoverlapping bridge states that acquisitions add 100 and translation at current instead of prior rates adds 20; subtracting both produces current revenue on the prior perimeter and rate basis. Calculate growth after those two adjustments. Is exact same-52-week growth identified? Calculate it only under the additional assumption of uniform weekly revenue on that adjusted basis. Explain two further disclosures needed before calling either result an organic profitability improvement.
Complete solutions

  1. The provider label establishes neither IASB compliance nor SEC filing eligibility. Inspect the actual issuer, foreign-private-issuer status and filing, basis-of-preparation wording, jurisdictional endorsement and differences, the audit opinion and any required reconciliation. The SEC staff route is specifically IFRS as issued by the IASB; do not turn “based on” into an unreserved compliance statement. Obtain the annual-period start, the applicable adopted standard/version and any early-adoption disclosure. IFRS 18's mandatory date is periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027, with early application possible; a public page alone does not show 2025 adoption. Credit an answer that preserves unknowns and records the report/version and supporting paragraph instead of inventing a reconciliation of zero.

  2. Purchases follow the LIFO identity: 260 − 120 + 140 = 280. FIFO opening inventory is 150 and closing inventory 185; FIFO COGS is 150 + 280 − 185 = 245, equivalently 260 − (45−30). FIFO profit is 70 + 15 = 85. Opening equity increases 30 and closing equity 45, reconciled by the 15 profit increase. LIFO CFO is 70 − (140−120) = 50; FIFO CFO is 85 − (185−150) = 50. Cash, purchases and liabilities are unchanged. Adding the closing reserve to current profit would give 115 and improperly include the opening difference 30 again.

  3. Revenue is 450. FIFO consumes inventory 360, yielding profit 450 − 360 − 50 = 40; LIFO consumes inventory 200, yielding profit 200. Both end with zero inventory, so the reserve falls from 160 to zero: the FIFO profit adjustment is −160. CFO is 400 under both methods, either directly 450−50 or indirectly 40−(0−360) = 200−(0−200). Cash rises from 770 to 1170. Assets are cash 1170, liabilities 100 and equity 1070 under both bases. FIFO cumulative profit is 260+170+40=470; LIFO is 180+90+200=470, added to capital600. The higher LIFO X3 profit reflects release of older, lower costs; the physical sales and cash are identical.

  4. Original annual depreciation is (150−30)/6 = 20. After two years the carrying amount is 110. The remaining depreciable amount is 110−30=80; divide by the new two-year remaining life to get 40 annually. Current profit is 90−40=50 and CFO is 50+40=90. Prior annual depreciation remains20. The next two closing carrying amounts are70 then30. Evidence must show a genuinely new assessment or changed circumstances and that the earlier estimate reasonably used the information then available. A discovery that an original reliable input was misentered would call for error analysis instead; an unfavorable outcome alone is insufficient.

  5. Reported X1 profit was80, so opening-X2 RE was80; corrected X1 profit is70, so corrected opening-X2 RE is70. The corresponding machine balances are100 and90. Reported X2 profit80 becomes70; closing-X2 RE160 becomes140, and machine80 becomes60. At start X3, the cumulative correction debits RE20 and credits accumulated depreciation20; it does not reduce cash. The X2 comparative bridge allocates ten to its opening balance and ten to its own profit. X3 depreciation30 gives profit70. Charging prior20 as another X3 expense gives50, understates that year's profit and leaves the historical pattern uncorrected.

  6. Other included expenses are Hardware26 and Services34. External revenue is540−40=500. Segment profits54+36=90, less corporate20 and share compensation10, give operating profit60; interest8 gives PBT52; tax13 gives net income39. Assets are180+120+50−20=330. The sum of segment profits already includes the seller's internal revenue and buyer's equal internal expense. Removing both cancels; subtracting just40 again lowers profit incorrectly. Equivalently, external operating expense is(286+164−40)+20+10=440. Net income is not CFO: depreciation, working-capital changes, share compensation, tax payments and other noncash/timing items would need their own cash reconciliation; this packet does not supply it.

  7. Recast X1 A to240 and B to160. Growth is252/240−1=5% and168/160−1=5%; group growth is420/400−1=5%. Unrecast calculations give A −8/260≈−3.077% and B28/140=20%, mistaking reassignment for activity change. Group revenue remains400 in X1 and420 in X2; it needs no correction. Preserve the published segment labels and the mapping to the current structure so another analyst can reproduce both series.

  8. The documented prior-perimeter/prior-rate current revenue is660−100−20=540, giving8% growth relative to500. It still covers53 weeks. Without weekly or comparable-period data, exact same-52-week growth is not identified. Under the additional uniform-week assumption only, adjusted52-week revenue is540×52/53=28080/53≈529.811 and growth is79/1325≈5.9623%. Label this a model-based normalization, not an observed fact. Request the extra week's timing and seasonal sales pattern, price/volume/mix evidence, margin and cost changes on the same boundary, and the acquisition/translation methodology. Revenue growth alone establishes neither an underlying causal improvement nor profitability. Credit any two specific evidence requests linked to those uncertainties.

Teach-back and delayed retrieval

Teach-back. An analyst wants to add Orion's entire closing reserve to X2 profit, restate a properly estimated asset after new evidence, and call Vector's segment-profit sum net income. Explain the three corrections in two minutes, including one equation and one source/version check.

Teach-back criteria and illustrative answer

For the same inventory history, FIFO profit equals LIFO profit plus the change in reserve:90+(160−80)=170. Cash remains770 because the inventory adjustment offsets the profit adjustment in CFO. A new useful-life assessment applies to the remaining carrying amount prospectively; only a supported prior error leads to the illustrated comparative correction. Vector's90 must bridge through corporate20, share compensation10, interest8 and tax13 to39. Identify the report, accounting framework and effective version; the IAS8 web title or an issued IFRS18 page does not itself show adoption. Credit causal explanations and explicit assumptions, not only corrected numbers.

Delayed check, one week later. (1) State the stock/flow reserve distinction. (2) Rebuild Orion's X2 CFO on both bases. (3) Give History A's X3 depreciation and History B's cumulative prior correction. (4) Explain why changing Vector's matched internal transfer price changes segment profits but not group profit. (5) Name four fields that belong in every comparison record.

Delayed-check answers

(1) Ending R adjusts inventory and no-tax equity; ΔR adjusts period profit. (2) FIFO170−120=50; LIFO90−40=50. (3) New-estimate depreciation80/3; material-error correction reduces prior asset and RE by20 without changing cash. (4) A ten increase adds ten to seller profit and subtracts ten from buyer profit; both internal revenue and expense are eliminated, leaving group totals unchanged under the no-unsold-margin assumption. (5) Any four of entity/perimeter, dates/calendar, currency/units, exact framework/version/adoption, source-note/version and supported analytical treatment; an effective comparison also specifies the target definition and remaining unknowns.

Sources, limits and next step

Primary bodies were inspected on 8 October 2026 for this 6 October 2026 edition boundary: the IFRS Foundation's IAS 8, IAS 2, IFRS 8 and IFRS 18 public overviews; scoped dated AASB 108 and AASB 8 text; actual FASB 2015-11 and FASB 2023-07 amendment documents; and SEC staff manual section 6310. Full gated IFRS normative texts and the complete current FASB Codification were not inspected. These sources support the stated educational scope; they do not certify a reporting election or complete filing compliance. All numerical cases and problems are original and synthetic.

Forensic analysis and accounting integration uses these comparisons to investigate cash/profit gaps, business explanations and contractual risk. An unexplained difference is a reason to obtain evidence, not proof of misstatement or intent.

Sources and further study

  • IFRS Foundation — IAS 8, public overview (currently titled Basis of Preparation of Financial Statements) — Policy hierarchy and broad distinction between retrospective policy/error treatment and prospective new estimates; web title versus applicable reporting version.
  • IFRS Foundation — IAS 2 Inventories, public overview — FIFO and weighted-average formulas for interchangeable inventories; limited IFRS side of cost-basis comparison.
  • IFRS Foundation — IFRS 8 Operating Segments, public overview — Purpose and scope of activity/environment, product/geography/customer information; route to deeper segment analysis.
  • IFRS Foundation — IFRS 18 Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements, public overview — Effective annual periods beginning 1 January 2027, early application, replacement of IAS1 and relocation to IAS8; example of issued versus adopted requirements.
  • Australian Accounting Standards Board — AASB 108 March 2021 amendments compilation, operative for periods beginning 2023–2026 — Accessible jurisdiction-labeled detailed policy-change conditions, opening comparative/equity adjustments, evidence-dependent estimate/error distinction and correction disclosure.
  • Australian Accounting Standards Board — AASB 8 March 2020 amendments compilation, operative from July 2021 to before January 2027 — Operating-segment/CODM definition, measurement boundaries, group reconciliations and comparative segment composition.
  • Financial Accounting Standards Board — ASU 2015-11, Inventory (Topic 330): Simplifying the Measurement of Inventory, July 2015 — Primary U.S. amendment evidence for the LIFO/non-LIFO distinction; distinguishes an ASU communication from authoritative Codification.
  • Financial Accounting Standards Board — ASU 2023-07, Segment Reporting (Topic 280): Improvements to Reportable Segment Disclosures, November 2023 — Public-entity segment expense/other-item disclosures, management measures, reconciliation and dated annual/interim transition scope.
  • U.S. SEC Division of Corporation Finance — Financial Reporting Manual, Topic 6, section 6310 — Scoped foreign-private-issuer IFRS-as-issued-by-IASB reconciliation accommodation and required compliance evidence; jurisdiction and issuer status matter.
